title: GOD KEPT USING SAMSON… EVEN WHILE SAMSON KEPT DESTROYING HIMSELF. WHY?
paragraphs: GOD KEPT USING SAMSON… EVEN WHILE SAMSON KEPT DESTROYING HIMSELF. WHY?
The terrifying truth behind a man who broke his vows, surrendered to his desires, lost his strength, and discovered that God's mercy could reach him even in the wreckage of his own choices.
What if the most frightening thing about Samson's story isn't that he lost his strength… but that he had been losing himself long before he realized God had departed from him?
Not because it describes a demon.
Not because it announces judgment upon an entire nation.
But because it describes a man who once carried the power of God.
A man who had torn apart a lion with his bare hands.
A man who had defeated enemies that ordinary soldiers feared.
A man whose birth had been announced by an angel.
And yet, one morning, he woke up believing everything was still the same.
He thought he could rise.
He thought he could fight.
He thought the power would come again.
But Scripture records something devastating.
“And he wist not that the LORD was departed from him.” — Judges 16:20 (KJV)
Read that again.
He did not know.
Samson had become so accustomed to living with compromise that he failed to recognize the moment his spiritual condition had reached a catastrophic turning point.
And perhaps that is why his story is not merely about a strong man who fell.
It is about the terrifying possibility of becoming comfortable with what is destroying us.
Still attending church.
Still knowing the worship songs.
Still quoting Scripture.
Still speaking about God.
Still remembering the victories of yesterday.
While quietly making peace with the very things we once begged God to deliver us from.
And the question becomes almost unbearable.
Why did God permit Samson to remain a judge over Israel despite his repeated moral failures?
Why did God continue working through a man who repeatedly demonstrated such poor judgment?
Why wasn't Samson immediately replaced?
Why did a holy God accomplish His purposes through someone whose personal life was so deeply compromised?
And perhaps the question beneath all those questions is even more personal.
If God knew everything Samson would become, why did He call him in the first place?
The answer takes us into one of the most uncomfortable and hope-filled accounts in the Old Testament.
Because Samson's story reveals both the seriousness of sin and the astonishing sovereignty of God.
And when we finally understand what happened between his miraculous birth and his final prayer, we discover something that points beyond Samson himself.
We discover why even the strongest human deliverer was never enough.
We discover why Israel needed Jesus.
And why we still do.
Before Samson ever opened his eyes, Israel was already in trouble.
Judges 13:1 tells us that the Israelites had again done evil in the sight of the LORD, and God had delivered them into the hands of the Philistines for forty years.
Forty years.
An entire generation growing up beneath foreign domination.
Children learning to live under oppression.
Families adjusting to conditions that should never have become normal.
And unlike some earlier accounts in Judges, chapter 13 records no national cry for deliverance before God announces Samson's birth.
That detail matters.
God initiates the deliverance.
Not because Israel has suddenly become righteous.
Not because its people have demonstrated extraordinary faithfulness.
But because the LORD remains sovereign over His covenant purposes.
Then an angel appears to a woman who has been unable to conceive.
Her barrenness is about to become the setting for an extraordinary act of God.
The angel announces that she will bear a son who must be set apart to God from the womb.
And then comes the declaration that defines Samson's calling.
“And he shall begin to deliver Israel out of the hand of the Philistines.” — Judges 13:5 (KJV)
Notice one word.
Begin.
Not complete.
Not permanently liberate.
Begin.
In the Hebrew text, the verb is יָחֵל (yāḥēl), meaning “he will begin.”
Samson was not promised the complete overthrow of Philistine domination.
His calling was to initiate a work of deliverance within God's larger purpose.
That means Samson's mission was never dependent upon his becoming a flawless national hero.
But neither did God's purpose give Samson permission to live carelessly.
There is a profound difference between God's ability to accomplish His purposes through imperfect people and God's approval of their imperfections.
God's sovereignty is not the same as God's endorsement.
And if we miss that distinction, we will misunderstand everything that follows.
Samson was to be a Nazirite, a person specially consecrated to God.
The Hebrew term נָזִיר (nāzîr) carries the idea of someone separated or consecrated.
Numbers 6 describes the ordinary Nazirite regulations, including abstaining from products of the vine, not cutting one's hair, and avoiding contact with the dead.
Samson's consecration was unusual because it was announced before his birth and intended to last throughout his life.
His uncut hair was an outward sign of that consecration.
It was not a magical source of supernatural energy.
God Himself was the source of Samson's strength.
Judges 13:25 tells us that the Spirit of the LORD began to move him.
Judges 14:6, 14:19, and 15:14 describe extraordinary moments when the Spirit of the LORD came powerfully upon him.
This is essential to understanding the story.
Samson's power was a divine gift connected to his God-given calling.
It was not proof that every decision he made was pleasing to God.
And this is where the account begins to confront us.
Because it is possible to possess remarkable gifts while displaying deeply troubling character.
It is possible to have a genuine calling and still make destructive choices.
It is possible for God to accomplish something through a person without approving of everything that person does.
The presence of a gift is not a certificate of personal holiness.
A powerful ministry does not excuse a private pattern of sin.
A public victory does not automatically mean a private life is healthy.
And yesterday's usefulness does not give anyone permission to disregard God's Word today.
Samson's tragedy begins with something that seems almost ordinary.
He sees a woman.
And he wants her.
In Judges 14, Samson goes down to Timnah, sees a Philistine woman, and demands that his parents arrange the marriage.
His parents object, asking why he must seek a wife among the uncircumcised Philistines.
But Samson insists.
“Get her for me; for she pleaseth me well.” — Judges 14:3 (KJV)
The Hebrew expression כִּי־הִיא יָשְׁרָה בְעֵינָי (kî-hîʾ yāšərāh bəʿênāy) communicates that she is right or pleasing in his eyes.
In the wider book of Judges, that language becomes especially significant.
The book eventually describes Israel's spiritual disorder with the repeated observation that everyone did what was right in his own eyes.
Samson's personal desires reflect something of the spiritual confusion surrounding him.
He sees.
He wants.
He insists.
And what makes this passage particularly challenging is Judges 14:4.
Scripture explains that Samson's parents did not know that the matter was from the LORD, who was seeking an occasion against the Philistines.
Does that mean God approved of Samson's attitude, every aspect of his romantic pursuit, or the destructive decisions that followed?
No.
The passage reveals God's sovereign purpose in bringing confrontation against the Philistines.
It does not turn every human motive involved into a righteous one.
God can govern events involving sinful human choices without becoming the author or moral approver of those sins.
This is not an excuse for Samson.
It is a revelation about God.
Human failure cannot overthrow divine sovereignty.
But divine sovereignty never makes human failure harmless.
And Samson would learn that through pain.
His wedding arrangements collapse into betrayal, anger, violence, and retaliation.
A riddle becomes a conflict.
A marriage becomes a disaster.
A cycle of revenge begins.
And with every escalation, Samson's extraordinary strength becomes more visible while his personal instability becomes harder to ignore.
He can defeat enemies.
But he struggles to govern his impulses.
He can break physical restraints.
But he repeatedly allows his desires to lead him into danger.
He can carry the gates of Gaza on his shoulders.
But he cannot seem to recognize how vulnerable he has become to his own appetites.
And perhaps that is where this ancient story becomes painfully modern.
Because some of us know what it means to appear strong while quietly losing battles nobody else can see.
You can be the person everyone calls for advice and still need someone to confront you.
You can encourage an entire room and return home to a temptation you have stopped resisting.
You can be gifted, respected, needed, and exhausted.
You can know exactly what Scripture says and still find yourself negotiating with something you know is wrong.
The danger is not merely that we are weak.
The danger is that we may begin treating God's patience as permission.
And that brings us back to the question.
Why did God allow Samson to continue?
First, because Samson's judgeship was not a modern public office with a recorded process of election, removal, and replacement.
The judges in Israel were deliverers and leaders raised up in particular circumstances.
Judges 15:20 and 16:31 report that Samson judged Israel for twenty years during the days of the Philistines.
The text does not record a formal hearing in which God repeatedly considered removing Samson from office and decided to retain him.
We must not invent one.

What Scripture does show is that God had announced a purpose for Samson before his birth, empowered him at decisive moments, and used his conflict with the Philistines as part of Israel's deliverance.
Yet Scripture also shows that Samson's moral failures brought terrible consequences.
God's patience was not indifference.
God's continued sovereignty was not moral approval.
And the fact that Samson remained a judge did not mean he escaped accountability.
In fact, his story demonstrates the opposite.
A person can continue to occupy a position while already moving toward the consequences of unrepented sin.
That should sober every leader.
Every preacher.
Every parent.
Every Christian who has mistaken God's delay in judgment for His approval of hidden compromise.
Samson's story does not teach us to celebrate gifted people regardless of their character.
It warns us against confusing visible effectiveness with spiritual maturity.
And then Delilah enters the story.
By Judges 16, Samson has already demonstrated a dangerous pattern of sexual recklessness.
The chapter first records his visit to a prostitute in Gaza.
Later, he loves a woman in the Valley of Sorek named Delilah.
The Philistine rulers offer Delilah silver to discover the secret of his strength.
She repeatedly asks him how he can be subdued.
Again and again, Samson gives misleading answers.
Again and again, she tests what he tells her.
And again and again, the warning signs become unmistakable.
This is what makes the narrative so painful.
Samson is not simply deceived by one unexpected betrayal.
He repeatedly exposes himself to a danger that is becoming increasingly obvious.
Eventually, under persistent pressure, he reveals the truth about his uncut hair and his consecration from birth.
While he sleeps, his hair is cut.
Then comes the cry.
“The Philistines be upon thee, Samson.”
And he awakens.
Confident.
Familiar with victory.
Expecting strength to return.
“I will go out as at other times before, and shake myself.” — Judges 16:20 (KJV)
But this time, something is different.
The LORD has departed from him.
The Philistines seize him.
They gouge out his eyes.
They bring him down to Gaza.
They bind him with bronze shackles.
And they force him to grind grain in prison.
The man who once moved with terrifying strength is now blind, restrained, and humiliated.
The man who had so often followed what pleased his eyes has lost his sight.
The man who had broken ropes is now bound.
The man who had defeated Philistines is now their captive.
And the Bible does not soften the tragedy.
Sin has consequences.
Sometimes devastating ones.
Not every consequence is immediate.
Not every warning is dramatic.
Sometimes the collapse comes after a long season of assuming we can keep living as before.
And I wonder how many people reading this are standing somewhere in that dangerous space.
Not yet exposed.
Not yet confronted.
Not yet experiencing the full consequences of a choice they know is wrong.
Perhaps nobody knows about the messages.
The dishonesty.
The bitterness.
The addiction.
The secret relationship.
The compromises you keep promising to end.
And because life has continued, you have begun to believe everything must be fine.
But Samson's story refuses to let us confuse delay with safety.
It asks a question that deserves more than a quick religious answer.
What are you continuing to entertain because you have not yet experienced its full cost?
If that question touches something you have been hiding, you do not need to explain the details publicly.
But you do need to bring them honestly before God.
Repentance is not merely feeling frightened by consequences.
It is turning from sin toward the God whose mercy we desperately need.
And there is a difference between being sorry that we were caught and grieving that we have sinned against the Lord.
Samson's account does not give us permission to postpone that turning.
It urges us to take God's warnings seriously while there is still time.
Yet just when the story seems to have reached its darkest point, Scripture gives us one quiet sentence.
One sentence that feels almost impossible to ignore.
“Howbeit the hair of his head began to grow again after he was shaven.” — Judges 16:22 (KJV)
His hair began to grow again.
Not his eyesight.
Not his freedom.
Not his reputation.
His hair.
The text does not say that growing hair automatically restored God's power.
It does not announce that all consequences had been reversed.
It simply tells us that the outward sign of his consecration began to return.
And within the unfolding story, that detail prepares us for what comes next.
There is something profoundly moving about the way Scripture places this sentence between Samson's humiliation and his final prayer.
The Philistines believe they have finished him.
His enemies celebrate.
His strength appears gone.
His life seems reduced to a spectacle.
But the story is not over.
And perhaps someone reading this needs to understand that the consequences of your past do not place you beyond the reach of God's mercy.
That does not mean every relationship will be restored.
It does not mean every lost opportunity will return.
It does not mean repentance erases earthly consequences.
It means that failure does not have to be the final word about your relationship with God.
You may have damaged something precious.
You may have ignored warnings.
You may be carrying regret that still hurts when the room becomes quiet.
But while you have breath, you can turn to the Lord.
Not because you deserve another opportunity.
But because God's mercy is greater than our ability to earn it.
Then comes Samson's final scene.
The Philistine rulers gather to celebrate their god Dagon, claiming that their god has delivered Samson into their hands.
They bring Samson out to entertain them.
The once-feared deliverer stands between the pillars of the building.
Blind.
Humiliated.
Dependent upon a young servant to guide him.
And there, in the middle of enemy celebration, Samson prays.
“O Lord GOD, remember me, I pray thee, and strengthen me, I pray thee, only this once, O God.” — Judges 16:28 (KJV)
The Hebrew begins:
אֲדֹנָי יְהוִה זָכְרֵנִי נָא
ʾĂdōnāy YHWH, zokhrēnî nāʾ.
“O Lord GOD, please remember me.”
The verb זָכְרֵנִי (zokhrēnî) means “remember me.”
In biblical prayer, asking God to remember someone is not suggesting that God has forgotten their existence.
It is an appeal for God to turn His attention toward them in mercy or action.
But we must be careful not to romanticize Samson's final prayer.
He also asks to be avenged for his eyes.
His words contain a personal desire for vengeance.
The passage does not explicitly describe a complete confession of every sin or a fully purified motive.
We should not claim more than Scripture reveals.
What we can say is that Samson finally appeals to the LORD for strength.
He no longer speaks as though he can simply rise and exercise power at will.
He asks.
And God grants him strength for one final act against the Philistine rulers.
Samson pushes against the supporting pillars.
The building collapses.
He dies along with those inside.
Judges 16:30 records that he killed more Philistines in his death than during his life.
His final act advances the conflict against Israel's oppressors, but it is also tragic and fatal.
This is not a model for Christians to imitate through violence or self-destruction.
It is a historical account of God's dealings with Israel during a particular period of redemptive history.
And it leaves us with a complicated man.
A divinely called deliverer.
A deeply flawed sinner.
A man whose failures were real.
A man whose strength was never truly his own.
A man whose final appeal to God was heard.
And then, centuries later, Scripture does something extraordinary.
In Hebrews 11, among the names associated with faith, we find Samson.
“And what shall I more say? for the time would fail me to tell of Gedeon, and of Barak, and of Samson, and of Jephthae…” — Hebrews 11:32 (KJV)
Samson.
The man who compromised.
The man who fell.
The man who lost his eyes.
The man who died beneath the ruins of a Philistine temple.
His name appears in a chapter celebrating faith.
Does that mean Hebrews approves of his moral failures?
Absolutely not.
Hebrews 11 does not declare Samson sinless.
It does not erase the warnings of Judges 13–16.
It does not turn his recklessness into righteousness.
It recognizes him among those whose stories testify to faith and God's work through human weakness.
The Greek word translated “faith” in Hebrews 11:1 is πίστις (pistis), a word associated with faith, trust, and confidence.
And the great surprise of Hebrews 11 is not that God found a collection of morally perfect people.
He did not.
It is that the biblical record of faith includes people whose lives reveal just how deeply human beings need God's grace.
Samson's inclusion reminds us that a person's worst failure does not necessarily exhaust everything God has done in their life.
But that truth must never become an excuse to keep sinning.
Romans 6:1–2 confronts that distortion directly.
“Shall we continue in sin, that grace may abound? God forbid.”
Grace does not invite us to become comfortable with the chains Christ came to break.
Grace calls us to repentance.
Grace teaches us to deny ungodliness, as Titus 2:11–12 explains.
Grace does not make holiness unnecessary.
Grace makes a transformed life possible.
And this is where Samson's story becomes much bigger than Samson.
Because if we finish the account merely saying, “God can still use broken people,” we have not yet reached its deepest significance.
The entire book of Judges exposes the insufficiency of human deliverers.
Israel repeatedly falls into evil.
Oppression follows.
God raises up deliverers.
Relief comes.
And the cycle returns.
Even the judges themselves are often deeply flawed.
Samson may be extraordinarily strong, but he cannot rescue Israel from the deepest problem afflicting the nation.
Sin.
And he cannot rescue himself from it either.
Israel needs more than a stronger warrior.
It needs a righteous King.
It needs a Deliverer whose obedience will not collapse beneath temptation.
A Savior who will not confuse personal desire with the will of God.
Someone who can confront evil without becoming enslaved to it.
Someone who can deal not merely with outward oppression but with the guilt and power of sin.
Israel needed Jesus Christ.
And so do we.
Consider the contrast.
Samson was set apart before birth for a particular mission.
Jesus was sent by the Father to accomplish the salvation of His people.
Samson repeatedly yielded to temptation.
Jesus was tempted, yet without sin (Hebrews 4:15).
Samson's strength was a gift he could not command independently of God.
Jesus, the eternal Son, willingly humbled Himself in obedience to the Father (Philippians 2:5–8).
Samson's final act brought judgment upon his enemies and cost him his life.
Jesus willingly gave His life for sinners, bearing our sins and securing redemption through His death and resurrection (1 Peter 2:24; 1 Corinthians 15:3–4).
These are not identical deaths.
Samson's death involved vengeance and the destruction of Philistine rulers.
Christ's death was the once-for-all sacrifice for sins, accomplished by the sinless Savior.
The difference matters.
Samson was a temporary, imperfect deliverer.
Jesus is the perfect and sufficient Savior.
Samson could begin a deliverance from Philistine oppression.
Jesus came to save His people from their sins (Matthew 1:21).
And where Samson's story ends beneath the wreckage of a fallen building, the Gospel announces an empty tomb.
Jesus Christ is risen.
Death did not hold Him.
Sin did not defeat Him.
And everyone who repents and believes in Him receives forgiveness and the promise of eternal life.
This is the Gospel.
Not that God overlooks sin because people are talented.
Not that God rewards us for being religious.
Not that our good deeds outweigh our failures.
But that Jesus Christ, the righteous One, died for the unrighteous to bring us to God (1 Peter 3:18).
That is why the answer to Samson's story is not greater confidence in our own strength.
It is surrender to Jesus Christ.
Perhaps you have spent years trying to prove that you are still strong.
Strong enough to hide the struggle.
Strong enough to control the temptation.
Strong enough to maintain the image.
Strong enough to keep everyone believing you are fine.
But the Christian life was never meant to be built upon pretending we do not need grace.
It is built upon the crucified and risen Christ.
The One who knows the truth about us.
The One who calls sinners to repentance.
The One who receives those who come to Him in faith.
The One who does not merely cover our shame with religious language but begins transforming us from within.
And perhaps the prayer you need tonight is not complicated.

“Lord Jesus, I have trusted my own strength for too long. I have excused things You have called me to surrender. Forgive me. Change my heart. Teach me to walk in truth. Help me turn away from what is destroying me. I do not want to hide behind my gifts, my reputation, or my past. I need Your grace. I need You.”
There is no magic in repeating those words.
Salvation is not earned by reciting a prayer.
But a heart that truly turns to Christ in repentance and faith will not find Him unwilling to save.
Jesus said:
“Him that cometh to me I will in no wise cast out.” — John 6:37 (KJV)
That promise is stronger than your shame.
And it is more trustworthy than your feelings.
Now I want to ask you something.
Not as someone trying to judge your past.
But as a fellow human being who understands how easy it is to look strong while carrying an invisible battle.
What part of Samson's story feels uncomfortably familiar?
Is it the repeated compromise?
The ignored warnings?
The temptation to mistake God's patience for approval?
The painful consequences?
Or the desperate realization that you need the Lord more than you ever admitted?
You do not have to disclose private sins or painful details to strangers.
Someone reading may need to know that a life surrendered to Jesus can truly change.
Not every testimony begins with a dramatic miracle.
Sometimes it begins with a quiet confession.
Sometimes it begins with an apology.
Sometimes it begins with deleting a number, telling the truth, seeking pastoral counsel, making restitution, or finally asking for help.
Sometimes it begins when a person stops defending what God is calling them to forsake.
And if this message has helped you see Scripture more clearly, please don't let it disappear into your feed.
Not because every word here is more important than Scripture, but because you may want to return to Judges 13–16 and examine these truths for yourself.
Perhaps there is a friend who has walked away from church because they believe their failures have disqualified them from ever coming back to God.
Perhaps there is a Christian leader quietly confusing ministry success with spiritual health.
Perhaps there is a son, a daughter, a spouse, or a friend who needs both the warning of Samson's collapse and the hope of Christ's mercy.

We want this community to be a place where biblical truth is taken seriously, where difficult passages are examined honestly, where sin is never celebrated, and where the grace of Jesus Christ is never treated as a small thing.
That is also why I want to share something personal about the mission behind Gospel Warrior.
Writing, researching, preparing, and distributing Christ-centered biblical teaching takes time, effort, and resources.
The Gospel is not merchandise.
God's forgiveness cannot be purchased.
Second Corinthians 9:7 reminds us that God loves a cheerful giver, not one pressured into giving.
Not guilt.
Not fear.
Not a promise that money will purchase God's blessing.
But a shared desire to make Christ known.
These free resources are part of our desire to make spiritual nourishment and Christian learning more accessible.
These items are simply a way to support and identify with the ministry's mission. They are not substitutes for prayer, Scripture, fellowship, or faithful obedience to Christ.
Because the goal is not to build a community impressed with Gospel Warrior.
The goal is to build a community increasingly devoted to Christ.
And that brings us to the question we began with.
Why did God permit Samson to remain a judge despite his repeated moral failures?
Because God had appointed Samson to begin a particular work of deliverance, and Scripture shows that His sovereign purposes continued even through Samson's deeply flawed life.
But God did not approve of Samson's sins.
He did not shield Samson from the consequences.
He did not present Samson as the perfect deliverer Israel needed.
Instead, the account exposes the weakness of human strength, the danger of compromise, the seriousness of sin, and the necessity of depending upon the LORD.
Samson's life was a warning.
His final appeal to God was a reminder that divine mercy is not exhausted by human failure.
And his inadequacy as a deliverer directs our attention toward the One who would never fail.
Jesus Christ.
So do not leave this story merely impressed by a man who tore down pillars.
Leave it asking whether you have been building your life upon a strength that cannot save you.
Do not wait until your world collapses before taking repentance seriously.
Do not mistake the gifts God has given you for permission to disregard His commands.
Do not confuse a platform with holiness.
Do not assume that because nobody sees your struggle, it is not shaping your soul.
And do not believe the lie that your past is stronger than the saving grace of Jesus Christ.
Come to Him.
Tell the truth.
Turn from sin.
Receive His forgiveness through faith.
And walk with Him, one day at a time.
Because the greatest miracle in this story is not that Samson could bring down a building.
It is that the God who worked through such a flawed deliverer would ultimately send His own sinless Son to accomplish a salvation no human judge could ever achieve.
Samson's strength could defeat enemies.
Only Jesus can save sinners.
And when you finally stop pretending you can rescue yourself, you may discover that the Savior you desperately need has been calling you to come to Him all along.
The tragedy is not that Samson finally discovered his weakness; it is that he spent so much of his life believing his strength was enough.
